title: Post Search
prompt: Design full-text search over the posts on a large social platform. A user types a few words and gets relevant posts back, including ones written seconds ago.

clarify.q: How fresh must results be: seconds, minutes, or hours?
clarify.why: Seconds means a near-real-time indexing path with small frequent segments. Hours would let us rebuild the index in batch and keep it read-only.

clarify.q: Is ranking by relevance, by recency, or a blend?
clarify.why: Pure recency lets us read posting lists newest-first and stop early. Relevance needs scoring every match, or a two-phase retrieve-then-rerank.

clarify.q: Do results depend on who is searching (private accounts, blocks)?
clarify.why: Per-user visibility turns a cacheable global query into a filtered one, and the filter has to run inside the index, not after.

clarify.q: How big is the corpus and how far back do people search?
clarify.why: If 80% of searches only care about the last week, a small hot index can serve most traffic and the old index can be slower and cheaper.

clarify.q: What languages, and do we need phrase or prefix search?
clarify.why: Languages decide tokenizers (CJK has no spaces). Phrase search needs term positions in the postings, which roughly doubles index size.

clarify.q: How quickly must edits and deletes disappear from results?
clarify.why: Deleted or privated posts showing up is a trust and legal issue. That pushes delete handling to the same fast path as inserts.

functional: Search posts by keywords; results ranked by a blend of text relevance, recency and engagement.
Filters: author, date range, language, has-media.
A new post is searchable within 5 s; a deleted post disappears within 5 s.
Paginate with a cursor; show a result count estimate.
Respect visibility: never return posts from private accounts the searcher cannot see, or from authors who blocked them.
nonFunctional: Search p99 under 300 ms end to end, p50 under 80 ms.
99.9% availability; partial results (one shard missing) are better than an error.
Index is derived data: it can always be rebuilt from the post store.
Indexing keeps up with 3× normal write peaks without raising freshness above 30 s.
outOfScope: Autocomplete and query suggestions (separate typeahead service).
Searching users or hashtags as entities.
Personalised ranking models and ads in results.
Semantic or vector search (mentioned as a follow-up).

assumptions: 100 M daily active users, 3 searches each per day
100 M new posts per day; 10 B posts kept searchable
Average post ≈ 200 bytes of text, ≈ 25 unique terms
Compressed posting ≈ 4 bytes (delta-coded doc ID + term frequency)
Per-document ranking columns ≈ 50 bytes (time, author, likes, language)

steps.label: Index size
steps.math: 10 B docs × 25 × 4 B = 1 TB postings; + 10 B × 50 B = 0.5 TB columns

steps.label: Shard count
steps.result: 100 shards, each small enough to rebuild in minutes

steps.label: Fan-out cost (document sharding)
steps.math: 10 k QPS × 100 shards = 1 M shard queries/s; × ~1 ms CPU = 1 000 cores

steps.label: Disk per node
steps.result: Index fits in page cache: CPU, not disk, sets node count

steps.label: With a 7-day hot tier
steps.math: 7 d × 100 M = 700 M docs ≈ 7 shards. 80% of 10 k QPS × 7 = 56 k; 20% × 93 = 186 k; total ≈ 242 k shard queries/s
steps.result: ≈ 4× less fan-out work than querying all 100 shards

estimates.takeaway:
Indexing is easy: ~1.2 k docs/s is tiny. The cost is on the query side. With document sharding every query visits every shard, so the cluster is sized by CPU for fan-out, not by storage. The whole index is ~4.5 TB with replicas and fits in memory across the nodes.

That makes two levers matter most: a small recent-posts tier that most queries stop at, and early termination inside each shard. Splitting by time cuts total shard work about 4×.

api.returns: 200 { results: [{ postId, snippet, author, createdAt, score }], nextCursor, approxTotal, partial }
api.note: partial=true when a shard timed out. The cursor encodes the last (score, postId) plus a snapshot token so pages stay stable.

api.body: { postId, version, authorId, text, lang, visibility, createdAt }
api.note: version is the post's update counter. Indexers ignore events older than what they already applied.
Deletes take the same fast path as inserts so removed posts disappear within seconds.
Internal scatter call; each shard returns its local top k within the deadline.

entities.name: Posting list
fields: only if we support phrase search
entities.why: The core structure: for each term, the sorted list of documents containing it. Queries become intersections and unions of these lists.

entities.name: Term dictionary
entities.why: Maps a query term to its posting list in one lookup. Kept in memory as a sorted or FST-style structure.

entities.name: Doc columns
fields: ranking signal, updated in place or via side table
entities.why: Ranking and filters need a few fields per matching doc, read column by column for speed.

entities.name: Live-docs bitmap
fields: which commit this bitmap belongs to
entities.why: Segments are immutable, so a delete or edit only flips a bit. Merges later drop the dead docs.

data.note:
The post store (sharded relational or wide-column) is the source of truth. The search index is a read model built from its change events: a CQRS split. Each shard holds a set of immutable segments plus one small in-memory buffer. New docs go to the buffer; every ~1 s the buffer is flushed into a new small segment that becomes searchable. Background merges combine small segments into larger ones, much like LSM compaction.

Documents are routed to shards by hash(postId) mod 100 inside each time tier, so writes go to one shard and load is even.

hld.summary:
Writes: the post service writes the post and an outbox row in one transaction. A relay publishes the change to a log topic partitioned by postId. Indexer workers consume it, tokenize the text, and send the document to the owning shard's primary. The primary appends to its translog for durability, adds the doc to its in-memory buffer, and replicates to its replicas. A refresh every second makes new segments searchable.

Reads: a stateless query service parses the query, picks tiers from the date filter (recent tier first), and scatters to one replica of every shard in that tier with a deadline. Each shard returns its local top k. The query service merges, optionally reranks the top few hundred, applies visibility checks, and hydrates snippets from the post cache.

diagram.title: Indexing pipeline and query path
diagram.src:
flowchart LR
  PS[Post service] --> PDB[(Post store)]
  PS --> OB[Outbox relay]
  OB --> LOG[Change log topic]
  LOG --> IDX[Indexer workers]
  IDX --> HOT["Recent tier (7 shards)"]
  IDX --> OLD["Archive tier (93 shards)"]
  U[Client] --> QS[Query service]
  QS --> HOT
  QS --> OLD
  QS --> RR[Reranker]
  QS --> PC[(Post cache)]
  QS --> VIS[Visibility service]

flows.title: A new post becomes searchable
steps: Post service commits the post and an outbox row in one transaction.
Relay publishes post.upserted to the change log, keyed by postId.
Indexer tokenizes (language detection, normalization, stemming) and sends the doc to the owning recent-tier shard.
Shard primary appends to its translog, adds to the memory buffer, and forwards to replicas.
Within ~1 s a refresh turns the buffer into a searchable segment; end-to-end lag is ~2–5 s.

flows.title: Running a query
steps: Query service parses "rust async runtime" into terms and filters, and checks a 30 s result cache for popular queries.
It sends Shard.Search to one replica of each recent-tier shard with a 100 ms deadline.
Each shard intersects posting lists, scores matches with BM25 plus recency, and returns its top 200.
If fewer than 20 good hits come back, or the date filter needs it, it queries the archive tier too.
It merges, reranks the top 200 with engagement signals, drops posts the searcher cannot see, and hydrates 20 results.

flows.title: A post is deleted
steps: post.deleted with a new version goes through the same log.
The owning shard flips the doc's bit in the live-docs bitmap; it vanishes at the next refresh.
A later merge physically removes it; until then it only costs a little disk.

deepDives.title: Inside a shard: the inverted index
deepDives.problem: A query like rust async must find the posts containing both words among ~100 M docs on a shard in about a millisecond. Scanning documents is impossible. We also need cheap appends at 1 k+ docs/s and deletes, while readers run in parallel.

options.name: Mutable B-tree of (term, docId)
options.how: One big sorted structure updated in place, like a database index.
pros: Updates and deletes in place
Familiar
cons: Random writes and locks on popular terms
Poor compression; much more memory per posting

options.name: Immutable segments plus merges
options.how: Buffer new docs in memory, flush to small immutable segments, search all segments, and merge them in the background. Deletes are bits in a live-docs bitmap.
pros: Lock-free reads: a segment never changes once written
Excellent compression (delta + bit-packing, ~4 B per posting)
Sequential I/O for writes and merges
cons: Each query visits several segments until merges catch up
Edits are delete + reinsert
Merge I/O must be throttled to protect query latency

deepDives.choice:
Immutable segments, as Lucene-style engines do. Query evaluation works on sorted posting lists: intersect the shortest list first and use skip pointers to jump through the longer one. With a top-k heap and per-block max scores, a shard can stop once no remaining doc can beat the current kth score. That is where the ~1 ms per shard-query comes from.

For our recency-heavy ranking, the recent tier stores doc IDs in time order, so walking lists newest-first finds good results early. Phrase search would need positions, roughly doubling index size. I would add positions only if product asks for exact quotes.

deepDives.title: Sharding: by document or by term
deepDives.problem: The index has to be split across machines. Splitting by document keeps writes local but sends every query to every shard. Splitting by term sends a query only to the shards owning its terms, but a single document's write touches many shards.

options.name: Document-partitioned
options.how: Each shard holds a full mini-index for a subset of posts (hash of postId). Queries scatter to all shards and gather top k.
pros: A post's write touches one shard
Hot terms spread evenly across shards
Shards are independent and easy to rebuild or move
cons: Every query costs N shard lookups (1 M/s at peak)
Tail latency follows the slowest shard

options.name: Term-partitioned
options.how: Each shard owns all postings for a range of terms. A two-word query hits at most two shards.
pros: Few shards per query
Good when queries are long and corpus is small
cons: One post updates ~25 shards
Very common terms make hot shards
Multi-term intersections must ship large posting lists across the network

options.name: Document-partitioned plus time tiers
options.how: Split by document inside each tier; tiers by post age. Queries hit the recent tier first and go deeper only if needed.
pros: Most queries touch 7 shards, not 100
Archive tier can use fewer replicas and cheaper hardware
cons: Ranking must merge across tiers
Daily roll-over of docs from recent to archive

deepDives.choice:
Document partitioning with time tiers. Term partitioning fails our freshness goal (each post updates ~25 shards) and creates hot shards for common words. Document partitioning is CPU-bound by fan-out, about 1 M shard-queries/s at peak, and tiering brings that to ~242 k.

To fight tail latency, use per-shard deadlines, hedged requests to a second replica after the p95, and return partial results with partial=true instead of failing. If the corpus were small and queries long, such as patent search, term partitioning would deserve a second look.

diagram.title: Scatter-gather with a deadline
diagram.src:
sequenceDiagram
  participant Q as Query service
  participant S1 as Shard 1
  participant S2 as Shard 2
  participant S7 as Shard 7
  Q->>S1: search top 200, deadline 100 ms
  Q->>S2: search top 200, deadline 100 ms
  Q->>S7: search top 200, deadline 100 ms
  S1-->>Q: local top 200
  S2-->>Q: local top 200
  Note over Q,S7: shard 7 slow, hedge to its replica
  S7-->>Q: local top 200
  Q->>Q: merge, rerank, cut to 20

deepDives.title: Indexing pipeline and freshness
deepDives.problem: Posts must be searchable within 5 s and deletes must vanish just as fast. The pipeline must not lose events, must handle out-of-order updates to the same post, and must let us rebuild the whole index when the analyzer changes.

options.name: Dual write from the post service
options.how: Post service writes the database, then calls the search cluster.
pros: Lowest latency
No extra infrastructure
cons: Crash between the two writes leaves them out of sync forever
Search outages slow down posting

options.name: Outbox or CDC to a log, then indexers
options.how: Changes go to a durable log partitioned by postId; indexers consume and apply with version checks.
pros: No lost updates; replayable
Search can be down without blocking posting
Same log feeds full rebuilds
cons: Adds a hop: ~1–2 s of extra lag
Need idempotent, version-checked writes

options.name: Periodic batch rebuild only
options.how: Rebuild segments from a snapshot every few hours.
pros: Simplest, very compact index
cons: Fails the 5 s freshness requirement

deepDives.choice:
Outbox to a log, partitioned by postId so all versions of one post arrive in order at one indexer. Each write carries the post's version, and the shard ignores anything older than what it has. Refresh every 1 s on the recent tier and every 30 s on the archive tier, where freshness hardly matters and fewer tiny segments means less merge work.

For analyzer changes or reshards, build a new index in parallel from a snapshot, replay the log from the snapshot's offset until it catches up, then switch an alias. If freshness were relaxed to minutes, I would refresh less often and save a lot of merge I/O.

deepDives.title: Ranking without blowing the latency budget
deepDives.problem: Text relevance alone surfaces old spam that repeats keywords. Recency alone surfaces noise. Engagement signals change by the second. Scoring every matching doc with a heavy model is too slow when a common term matches millions of posts.

options.name: Single-phase scoring in the shard
options.how: Each shard computes BM25 × recency decay + log(likes) for every match.
pros: Simple; one round trip
cons: Every signal must live in the shard
Can only use cheap formulas

options.name: Two-phase: retrieve then rerank
options.how: Shards return their top 200 by a cheap score; the query service reranks the merged ~1 400 candidates with richer features.
pros: Expensive model runs on a few hundred docs, not millions
Signals like author quality or spam score can live outside the index
cons: Good docs ranked below 200 in a shard are never seen
Extra ~20–40 ms for feature fetch and model

deepDives.choice:
Two-phase. Phase one in the shard: BM25 for text match, times an exponential recency decay, plus a small log-scaled engagement term, with early termination. Phase two: rerank ~1 400 candidates (7 shards × 200) with a learned model using author reputation, spam score and click feedback, within 40 ms.

Like counts in the shard are refreshed in batches every few minutes, not per like, because they are only a tie-breaker in phase one. If we added personalisation, it would go in phase two, which keeps the index global and cacheable.

failures: One shard replica is slow (GC pause, merge storm)
Per-shard deadline plus hedged request to another replica after the p95; return partial results flagged as partial.
Indexers fall behind and freshness climbs past 30 s
Alert on consumer lag in seconds; autoscale indexers; throttle archive-tier merges; recent tier gets priority.
A replica is promoted; un-flushed docs are recovered from the translog or replayed from the change log offset.
A bad analyzer deploy corrupts tokens
Index is derived: build a new index version from snapshot plus log replay and switch the alias back. Never mutate the live index in place for analyzer changes.
Viral query (breaking news) hammers the same shards
Short-TTL result cache keyed by normalized query and filters; request coalescing so 5 k identical queries in a second cause one scatter.
Visibility is checked at hydration against the post store as a backstop, so a lagging index never leaks a deleted or private post.
scale: 10× queries: add replicas, since the index is small. Cost scales with fan-out, so push more traffic to the recent tier and cache hot queries.
10× corpus: the archive tier grows to ~1 000 shards. Split it into yearly tiers and query older years only when asked, or route by date filters.
Multi-region: each region runs its own full index fed from a replicated change log, which keeps queries local. Freshness across regions is bounded by log replication lag.

followups.q: How do you support searching in Japanese or Chinese?
answer: No spaces between words, so use a dictionary-based segmenter or character bigrams per language.
Detect language at index time and store per-language fields with their own analyzer.
At query time run the same analyzer for the detected query language, and fall back to bigrams if unsure.

followups.q: How do you give a stable 'page 2'?
answer: Cursor holds the last (score, postId) and a point-in-time snapshot token.
Shards keep that segment set alive for a few minutes so new posts do not shift pages.
Deep paging past ~1 000 results is capped. Nobody reads it and it costs every shard.

followups.q: How would you add semantic search?
answer: Compute an embedding per post in the indexing pipeline and store it in an ANN index per shard.
Run lexical and vector retrieval in parallel, then fuse their candidates before the reranker.
Embeddings add ~1–3 KB per post, so 10 B posts means 10–30 TB. Start with the recent tier only.

followups.q: Why not just use the main database's full-text index?
answer: Works up to tens of millions of rows; at 10 B posts the ranking, fan-out and analyzers outgrow it.
Search traffic would compete with the transactional workload.
A separate read model lets us shard and tune search independently.

followups.q: How do you enforce blocks and private accounts?
answer: Index a visibility field and filter public-only inside shards for most queries.
For private accounts the searcher follows, pass a small allow-list of author IDs as a filter.
Final check at hydration against the post store as a safety net.

mistakes: Calling the search cluster directly from the write path and ignoring what happens if one of the two writes fails.
Picking term sharding without noticing every post write would touch ~25 shards.
Sizing the cluster by disk when the arithmetic says query fan-out CPU is the limit.
Treating deletes as an afterthought, so removed posts linger in results.
Describing ranking as 'use machine learning' with no first-phase retrieval and no latency budget.
